title: False Conversion
description: The formal fallacy where the subject and the predicate terms of the proposition are switched (*conversion*) in the conclusion, in a proposition that uses “all” in its premise (type “A” forms), or “some/not” (type “O” forms).
logical_form:
All P are Q.

Therefore, all Q are P.

Some P are not Q.

Therefore, some Q are not P.

examples.example:
All Hollywood Squares contestants are bad actors.

Therefore, all bad actors are Hollywood Squares contestants.

**Example #2:**

Some people in the film industry do not win Oscars.

Therefore, some Oscar winners are not people in the film industry.
examples.explanation: It does not follow logically that just because all *Hollywood Square*s contestants are bad actors that all bad actors actually make it on *Hollywood Squares*.  Same form problem with the second example -- but we used “some” and “are not”.

exceptions:
None, but remember that type “E” and type “I” forms can use conversion and remain valid.

No teachers are psychos.

Therefore, no psychos are teachers.
tips: Remember that formal fallacies are often obscured by unstructured rants. Creating a formal argument from such rants is both an art and a science.
references: Welton, J. (1896). *A Manual of Logic*. W. B. Clive.
